claim: Kisspeptin (Kiss1) and neurokinin B (NKB) neurocircuits are essential for pubertal development and fertility.
source: Kisspeptin (Kiss1) and neurokinin B (NKB) neurocircuits are essential for pubertal development and fertility.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Kiss1 and NKB neurocircuits.

claim: Kisspeptin neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (Kiss1ARH) co-express Kiss1, NKB, dynorphin and glutamate.
source: Kisspeptin neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (Kiss1ARH) co-express Kiss1, NKB, dynorphin and glutamate and are postulated to provide an episodic, excitatory drive to gonadotropin-releasing hormone 1 (GnRH) neurons, the synaptic mechanisms of which are unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of Kiss1ARH neurons.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons are postulated to provide an episodic, excitatory drive to GnRH neurons.
source: Kisspeptin neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (Kiss1ARH) co-express Kiss1, NKB, dynorphin and glutamate and are postulated to provide an episodic, excitatory drive to gonadotropin-releasing hormone 1 (GnRH) neurons, the synaptic mechanisms of which are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a postulate in the abstract, indicating it is a hypothesis based on existing knowledge.

claim: High-frequency photostimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons evoked local release of excitatory (NKB) and inhibitory (dynorphin) neuropeptides.
source: High-frequency photostimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons evoked local release of excitatory (NKB) and inhibitory (dynorphin) neuropeptides, which were found to synchronize the Kiss1ARH neuronal firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments using optogenetics and electrophysiology.

claim: NKB and dynorphin released from Kiss1ARH neurons synchronize Kiss1ARH neuronal firing.
source: High-frequency photostimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons evoked local release of excitatory (NKB) and inhibitory (dynorphin) neuropeptides, which were found to synchronize the Kiss1ARH neuronal firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Light-evoked synchronous activity of Kiss1ARH neurons caused robust excitation of GnRH neurons by a synaptic mechanism.
source: The light-evoked synchronous activity caused robust excitation of GnRH neurons by a synaptic mechanism that also involved glutamatergic input to preoptic Kiss1 neurons from Kiss1ARH neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Excitation of GnRH neurons involves glutamatergic input to preoptic Kiss1 neurons from Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: The light-evoked synchronous activity caused robust excitation of GnRH neurons by a synaptic mechanism that also involved glutamatergic input to preoptic Kiss1 neurons from Kiss1ARH neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons play a dual role of driving episodic secretion of GnRH through the differential release of peptide and amino acid neurotransmitters.
source: We propose that Kiss1ARH neurons play a dual role of driving episodic secretion of GnRH through the differential release of peptide and amino acid neurotransmitters to coordinate reproductive function.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Pulsatile secretion of GnRH is required for normal reproductive function.
source: Pulsatile secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone 1 (GnRH), and consequently pulsatile release of pituitary luteinizing hormone (LH), is required for normal reproductive function, and there is increasing evidence that kisspeptin (Kiss1) neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARH) are a component of the "GnRH pulse generator" (Navarro et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2011a; Lehman et al., 2010a; Okamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Kiss1 neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARH) are a component of the GnRH pulse generator.
source: Pulsatile secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone 1 (GnRH), and consequently pulsatile release of pituitary luteinizing hormone (LH), is required for normal reproductive function, and there is increasing evidence that kisspeptin (Kiss1) neurons in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (ARH) are a component of the "GnRH pulse generator" (Navarro et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2011a; Lehman et al., 2010a; Okamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from the literature.

claim: The GnRH pulse generator consists of bursts of multiunit activity (MUA) in the arcuate nucleus that are timed with pulses of LH secretion.
source: The "GnRH pulse generator" consists of bursts of multiunit activity (MUA) in the arcuate nucleus that are timed with pulses of LH secretion, and this phenomenon has been demonstrated in the monkey (Knobil, 1989), goat (Wakabayashi et al., 2010; Okamura et al., 2013), and rat (Kimura et al., 1991; Kinsey-Jones et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from multiple species.

claim: Two major populations of kisspeptin-synthesizing neurons exist in mammals - one in the anterior preoptic area and the other in the ARH.
source: In mammals, two major populations of kisspeptin-synthesizing neurons exist - one in the anterior preoptic area and the other in the ARH (Lehman et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: In rodents, the anterior preoptic cell group is a periventricular continuum within the anteroventral periventricular nucleus (AVPV) and the periventricular preoptic nucleus (PeN).
source: In rodents, the anterior preoptic cell group is a periventricular continuum within the anteroventral periventricular nucleus (AVPV) and the periventricular preoptic nucleus (PeN) and is responsible for the GnRH/LH surge (Clarkson and Herbison, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The AVPV/PeN Kiss1 neuron population is responsible for the GnRH/LH surge in rodents.
source: In rodents, the anterior preoptic cell group is a periventricular continuum within the anteroventral periventricular nucleus (AVPV) and the periventricular preoptic nucleus (PeN) and is responsible for the GnRH/LH surge (Clarkson and Herbison, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons co-synthesize and potentially co-release neurokinin B (NKB) and dynorphin (Dyn) in most mammals.
source: Both the AVPV/PeN and ARH Kiss1 neurons (Kiss1AVPV/PeN; Kiss1ARH) co-express other peptide and amino acid neurotransmitters, and the Kiss1ARH neurons co-synthesize and potentially co-release neurokinin B (NKB) and dynorphin (Dyn) in most mammals (Goodman et al., 2007; Navarro et al., 2011b; Bartzen-Sprauer et al., 2014), forming the basis for the "KNDy neuron" terminology (Lehman et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Kiss1, NKB and their respective receptors are absolutely essential for pubertal development and the control of reproduction.
source: Importantly, Kiss1, NKB and their respective receptors are absolutely essential for pubertal development and the control of reproduction (Seminara et al., 2003; d'Anglemont de Tassigny et al., 2007; Topaloglu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons can communicate with each other.
source: Morphological studies have provided evidence that Kiss1ARH neurons can communicate with each other (Lehman et al., 2010a; Rance et al., 2010; Navarro et al., 2011a; Navarro et al., 2011b), and NKB/tachykinin receptor 3 (Tacr3) and Dyn/κ-opioid receptor (KOR) signaling have been proposed to play a critical role in the generation of episodic GnRH/LH pulses via direct and synchronized action on GnRH nerve terminals in the median eminence (Navarro et al., 2009; Ohkura et al., 2009; Wakabayashi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from morphological studies.

claim: NKB/Tacr3 and Dyn/KOR signaling have been proposed to play a critical role in the generation of episodic GnRH/LH pulses via direct and synchronized action on GnRH nerve terminals in the median eminence.
source: Morphological studies have provided evidence that Kiss1ARH neurons can communicate with each other (Lehman et al., 2010a; Rance et al., 2010; Navarro et al., 2011a; Navarro et al., 2011b), and NKB/tachykinin receptor 3 (Tacr3) and Dyn/κ-opioid receptor (KOR) signaling have been proposed to play a critical role in the generation of episodic GnRH/LH pulses via direct and synchronized action on GnRH nerve terminals in the median eminence (Navarro et al., 2009; Ohkura et al., 2009; Wakabayashi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons are bilaterally interconnected within the ARH.
source: Anatomical tract-tracing studies have shown that Kiss1ARH neurons are bilaterally interconnected within the ARH and project to GnRH terminals in the median eminence and to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Rance et al., 2010; Yip et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from anatomical studies.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons project to GnRH terminals in the median eminence.
source: Anatomical tract-tracing studies have shown that Kiss1ARH neurons are bilaterally interconnected within the ARH and project to GnRH terminals in the median eminence and to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Rance et al., 2010; Yip et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from anatomical studies.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons project to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
source: Anatomical tract-tracing studies have shown that Kiss1ARH neurons are bilaterally interconnected within the ARH and project to GnRH terminals in the median eminence and to Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons (Rance et al., 2010; Yip et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations from anatomical studies.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons co-express the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vGluT2) and release the neurotransmitter glutamate.
source: Recent findings also indicate that Kiss1ARH neurons co-express the vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (vGluT2) and release the neurotransmitter glutamate (Cravo et al., 2011; Nestor et al., 2016), which could also provide an excitatory drive to hypothalamic neurons (Van den Pol et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: High-frequency photoactivation of Kiss1ARH neurons induced a NKB-mediated slow excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP).
source: We discovered that high-frequency photoactivation of Kiss1ARH neurons induced a NKB-mediated slow excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP), which was modulated by co-released dynorphin, and caused synchronization of Kiss1ARH neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: The NKB-mediated slow EPSP was modulated by co-released dynorphin.
source: We discovered that high-frequency photoactivation of Kiss1ARH neurons induced a NKB-mediated slow excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP), which was modulated by co-released dynorphin, and caused synchronization of Kiss1ARH neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: The NKB-mediated slow EPSP caused synchronization of Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: We discovered that high-frequency photoactivation of Kiss1ARH neurons induced a NKB-mediated slow excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP), which was modulated by co-released dynorphin, and caused synchronization of Kiss1ARH neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Activation of Kiss1ARH neurons co-released glutamate that excited the rostral Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
source: Interestingly, activation of Kiss1ARH neurons co-released glutamate that excited the rostral Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: The combination of synchronization and unified excitation of Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons resulted in robust excitation of GnRH neurons.
source: The combination of synchronization and unified excitation of Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons resulted in robust excitation of GnRH neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: A 10-s photostimulation at 1 or 5 Hz had no lasting effect on Kiss1ARH neuron activity.
source: A 10-s photostimulation at 1 or 5 Hz had no lasting effect on Kiss1ARH neuron activity; however, with 10 Hz stimulation there was a prominent depolarization of ~10 mV that peaked about a minute later, and it was accompanied by a train of action potentials during that time (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: 10 Hz photostimulation of Kiss1ARH neurons produced a prominent depolarization of ~10 mV that peaked about a minute later, accompanied by a train of action potentials.
source: A 10-s photostimulation at 1 or 5 Hz had no lasting effect on Kiss1ARH neuron activity; however, with 10 Hz stimulation there was a prominent depolarization of ~10 mV that peaked about a minute later, and it was accompanied by a train of action potentials during that time (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: 1 s of photostimulation at 20 Hz was ineffective in producing a depolarization in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: We also varied the duration of photostimulation at 20 Hz, which revealed that 1 s was ineffective but with 5 or 10 s of stimulation there was again a prominent depolarization accompanied by a barrage of action potentials that continued for about a minute after stimulation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: 5 or 10 s of photostimulation at 20 Hz produced a prominent depolarization accompanied by a barrage of action potentials that continued for about a minute after stimulation in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: We also varied the duration of photostimulation at 20 Hz, which revealed that 1 s was ineffective but with 5 or 10 s of stimulation there was again a prominent depolarization accompanied by a barrage of action potentials that continued for about a minute after stimulation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2F.

claim: A maximum depolarization of 22 ± 1.4 mV was obtained with a 10 s stimulation at 20 Hz in Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: The results from varying frequency and/or duration of photostimulation revealed that a maximum depolarization of 22 ± 1.4 mV was obtained with a 10 s stimulation at 20 Hz (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons had a transient hyperpolarization after 10-s stimulation at 20 Hz and a return to continuous firing ~30 s after the stimulation.
source: To determine whether the slow EPSP is a unique property of Kiss1ARH neurons, we also tested the AVPV/PeN population of Kiss1 neurons with 10-s stimulation at 20 Hz (Figure 2I); these neurons had a transient hyperpolarization after stimulation and a return to continuous firing ~30 s after the stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2I.

claim: POMC neurons fired action potentials during the 10-s, 20-Hz stimulation and exhibited a prolonged hyperpolarization afterwards.
source: The relatively quiescent POMC neurons fired action potentials during the 10-s, 20-Hz stimulation and exhibited a prolonged hyperpolarization afterwards (Figure 2J);
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2J.

claim: AgRP neurons exhibited a brief pause in firing in conjunction with a slight hyperpolarization after 10-s, 20-Hz stimulation.
source: whereas the spontaneously active AgRP neurons exhibited a brief pause in firing in conjunction with a slight hyperpolarization (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2K.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons are unique among the neurons tested in the generation of the slow EPSP.
source: Thus, Kiss1ARH neurons are unique among the neurons tested in the generation of the slow EPSP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing responses of different neuron types.

claim: The expression of Kiss1, dynorphin, NKB and Tacr3 are all down-regulated in kisspeptin neurons by E2-treatment.
source: Given that the expression of Kiss1, dynorphin, NKB and Tacr3 are all down-regulated in kisspeptin neurons by E2-treatment (Smith et al., 2005; Gottsch et al., 2009; Navarro et al., 2011a; Ruiz-Pino et al., 2012), we asked the question whether the slow EPSP would also be reduced by E2 or even vary during the ovulatory cycle.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The slow EPSP was most robust in OVX females (13.8 ± 1.6 mV, n= 17).
source: The slow EPSP was the most robust in OVX females (13.8 ± 1.6 mV, n= 17), which was to be expected if this current was peptidergic in nature—i.e., correlates with the up-regulation of NKB (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2L.

claim: In vivo E2 treatment resulted in a significant reduction of the slow EPSP amplitude (4.8 ± 1.1 mV, n = 9, p<0.001).
source: Moreover, in vivo E2 treatment resulted in a significant reduction of the slow EPSP amplitude (4.8 ± 1.1 mV, n = 9, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experiments with statistical significance.

claim: The slow EPSP was of greater magnitude in Kiss1ARH neurons from diestrous animals (9.2 ± 1.1 mV, n=14).
source: Importantly, the slow EPSP was also of greater magnitude in Kiss1ARHneurons from diestrous animals (9.2 ± 1.1 mV, n=14) and significantly reduced in Kiss1ARH neurons from proestrous animals (3.3 ± 0.8 mV, n=15, p<0.01) (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figure 2L.

claim: The slow EPSP was significantly reduced in Kiss1ARH neurons from proestrous animals (3.3 ± 0.8 mV, n=15, p<0.01).
source: Importantly, the slow EPSP was also of greater magnitude in Kiss1ARHneurons from diestrous animals (9.2 ± 1.1 mV, n=14) and significantly reduced in Kiss1ARH neurons from proestrous animals (3.3 ± 0.8 mV, n=15, p<0.01) (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experiments with statistical significance, with reference to Figure 2L.

claim: The slow EPSP was abolished by perfusing CSF containing low Ca2+ (0.5 mM) and high Mg2+ (10 mM).
source: The slow EPSP was abolished by perfusing CSF containing low Ca2+ (0.5 mM) and high Mg2+ (10 mM) or tetrodotoxin (TTX, 0.5 µM) (Figure 3B,D,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 3B, 3D, and 3F.

claim: The slow EPSP was abolished by tetrodotoxin (TTX, 0.5 µM).
source: The slow EPSP was abolished by perfusing CSF containing low Ca2+ (0.5 mM) and high Mg2+ (10 mM) or tetrodotoxin (TTX, 0.5 µM) (Figure 3B,D,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 3B, 3D, and 3F.

claim: TTX blockade of the light-induced response could be rescued with the addition of K+ channel blockers 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 0.5 mM) and tetraethylammonium (TEA, 7.5 mM).
source: We could rescue TTX blockade of the light-induced response with the addition of K+ channel blockers 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 0.5 mM) and tetraethylammonium (TEA, 7.5 mM) to facilitate ChR2- mediated depolarization of nerve terminals and neurotransmitter release (Cousin and Robinson, 2000; Petreanu et al., 2009), arguing that the response is dependent on direct pre-synaptic input from neighboring Kiss1 neurons (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 3C and 3F, and supporting citations.

claim: The slow EPSP is dependent on direct pre-synaptic input from neighboring Kiss1 neurons.
source: We could rescue TTX blockade of the light-induced response with the addition of K+ channel blockers 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 0.5 mM) and tetraethylammonium (TEA, 7.5 mM) to facilitate ChR2- mediated depolarization of nerve terminals and neurotransmitter release (Cousin and Robinson, 2000; Petreanu et al., 2009), arguing that the response is dependent on direct pre-synaptic input from neighboring Kiss1 neurons (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TTX rescue experiment.

claim: The majority of Kiss1ARH neurons are glutamatergic.
source: Although the majority of Kiss1ARH neurons are glutamatergic (Cravo et al., 2011), release glutamate locally in ARH (Nestor et al., 2016) and the fast EPSP was blocked by CNQX (10 µM) and AP5 (50 µM), the slow EPSP was unaffected by these ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Kiss1ARH neurons release glutamate locally in ARH.
source: Although the majority of Kiss1ARH neurons are glutamatergic (Cravo et al., 2011), release glutamate locally in ARH (Nestor et al., 2016) and the fast EPSP was blocked by CNQX (10 µM) and AP5 (50 µM), the slow EPSP was unaffected by these ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The fast EPSP in Kiss1ARH neurons was blocked by CNQX (10 µM) and AP5 (50 µM).

claim: The slow EPSP was unaffected by ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists CNQX (10 µM) and AP5 (50 µM).

evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: The expression of the slow EPSP was reduced but not blocked by QX314 (0.5 mM in the internal solution).
source: Action potentials were abrogated by dialyzing Kiss1ARH neurons with the Na+ channel blocker QX314 (0.5 mM in the internal solution) (Isaac and Wheal, 1993). The expression of the slow EPSP was reduced but not blocked by QX314 (Figure 4A,E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 4A and 4E.

claim: The reduction in the amplitude of the slow EPSP by QX314 was probably due to QX314 suppression of calcium currents in the Kiss1 neurons.
source: The reduction in the amplitude of the slow EPSP was probably due to QX314 suppression of calcium currents in the Kiss1 neurons (Hu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Postsynaptic electrical stimulation (20 Hz, 10 s) of individual Kiss1ARH neurons did not mimic the light-induced EPSP.
source: Moreover, postsynaptic electrical stimulation (20 Hz, 10 s) of individual neurons, even in the presence of 4-AP and TEA, did not mimic the light-induced EPSP (Figure 4B,C,E), suggesting that the response was not dependent on the generation of action potentials in the cell soma.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 4B, 4C, and 4E.

claim: The slow EPSP response was not dependent on the generation of action potentials in the cell soma.
source: Moreover, postsynaptic electrical stimulation (20 Hz, 10 s) of individual neurons, even in the presence of 4-AP and TEA, did not mimic the light-induced EPSP (Figure 4B,C,E), suggesting that the response was not dependent on the generation of action potentials in the cell soma.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrical stimulation experiment.

claim: Tacr1 and Tacr3, but not Tacr2, mRNA expression was measured in Kiss1ARH neurons using single cell RT-PCR.
source: We have measured Tacr1 and Tacr3, but not Tacr2, mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons using single cell RT-PCR (Navarro et al., 2015), and the Tacr3 agonist senktide depolarizes Kiss1ARH neurons (Navarro et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The Tacr3 agonist senktide depolarizes Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: We have measured Tacr1 and Tacr3, but not Tacr2, mRNA expression in Kiss1ARH neurons using single cell RT-PCR (Navarro et al., 2015), and the Tacr3 agonist senktide depolarizes Kiss1ARH neurons (Navarro et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Dialyzing Kiss1 neurons with GDP-β-S (2 mM in the internal solution) completely abrogated the slow EPSP response.
source: Firstly, in order to inhibit G protein activation we dialyzed Kiss1 neurons with the GDP analog GDP-β-S (Guanosine 5′-[β-thio]diphosphate trilithium, 2 mM in the internal solution) and completely abrogated the response (Figure 4D and E), demonstrating that the slow EPSP was mediated by a G protein-coupled receptor like Tacr3.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The slow EPSP was mediated by a G protein-coupled receptor like Tacr3.
source: Firstly, in order to inhibit G protein activation we dialyzed Kiss1 neurons with the GDP analog GDP-β-S (Guanosine 5′-[β-thio]diphosphate trilithium, 2 mM in the internal solution) and completely abrogated the response (Figure 4D and E), demonstrating that the slow EPSP was mediated by a G protein-coupled receptor like Tacr3.

claim: The slow EPSP was blocked by a Tacr3 antagonist SB222,200 (3 µM).

claim: The slow EPSP was blocked by a cocktail of antagonists against all 3 tachykinin receptors.

evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 5A, 5B, and 5D.

claim: The slow EPSP was occluded by pretreatment with Tacr3 agonist senktide.
source: The slow EPSP was also occluded by pretreatment with Tacr3 agonist senktide that depolarized Kiss1ARH neurons and pharmacologically prevented any effects of the photostimulated release of NKB (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with reference to Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Dual photostimulation induced desensitization similar to repeated senktide perfusion.
source: Finally, To see if dual photostimulation induced desensitization, we perfused senktide repeatedly (2x), and the averaged ratio of the responses (0.65 ± 0.01, n = 4) was similar to that obtained by photostimulation, suggesting that desensitization was caused by internalization and downregulation of Tacr3 following binding of NKB (Steinhoff et al., 2014) (Figure 5E,F).

claim: Desensitization was caused by internalization and downregulation of Tacr3 following binding of NKB.
source: Finally, To see if dual photostimulation induced desensitization, we perfused senktide repeatedly (2x), and the averaged ratio of the responses (0.65 ± 0.01, n = 4) was similar to that obtained by photostimulation, suggesting that desensitization was caused by internalization and downregulation of Tacr3 following binding of NKB (Steinhoff et al., 2014) (Figure 5E,F).

claim: Dynorphin is co-localized to over 90% of Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: Since dynorphin is co-localized to over 90% of Kiss1ARH neurons (Goodman et al., 2007; Navarro et al., 2009), and κ-opioid receptor mRNA is expressed in a subset of Kiss1ARH neurons (Navarro et al., 2009), we hypothesized that dynorphin would be co-released with high-frequency photostimulation and modulate NKB release from Kiss1 terminals.

claim: κ-opioid receptor mRNA is expressed in a subset of Kiss1ARH neurons.
source: Since dynorphin is co-localized to over 90% of Kiss1ARH neurons (Goodman et al., 2007; Navarro et al., 2009), and κ-opioid receptor mRNA is expressed in a subset of Kiss1ARH neurons (Navarro et al., 2009), we hypothesized that dynorphin would be co-released with high-frequency photostimulation and modulate NKB release from Kiss1 terminals.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Blockade of κ-opioid receptors by the selective antagonist nor-BNI (1 µM) potentiated the slow EPSP.

source: Finally, U69,593 (1 μM) reduced the frequency but not the amplitude of miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs); U69,593 did not alter the holding current (or input resistance) of Kiss1ARH neurons (Figure 6D–F).

claim: In both kisspeptin and histamine neurons there is glutamate-dependent (low-frequency) and peptide-dependent (high-frequency) release that transmit distinct postsynaptic excitatory effects.
source: Schöne et al. (2014) evoked a slow EPSC in tuberomammillary histamine neurons following high-frequency (≥20 Hz) photostimulation of ChR2-expressing orexin neurons that was abrogated by a selective orexin receptor two antagonist. Therefore, in both kisspeptin and histamine neurons there is glutamate-dependent (low-frequency) and peptide-dependent (high-frequency) release that transmit distinct postsynaptic excitatory effects; but in the case of Kiss1ARH neurons, it is a recurrent auto-excitation that allows recruitment of neighboring Kiss1ARH neurons for synchronizing firing.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn with a cited study.

claim: In Kiss1ARH neurons, it is a recurrent auto-excitation that allows recruitment of neighboring Kiss1ARH neurons for synchronizing firing.

source: Hence, Kiss1ARH neurons probably play a dual role of driving pulsatile (episodic) secretion of GnRH through kisspeptin release into the external zone of the median eminence, but also excite Kiss1AVPV/PeN neurons via glutamate release to help generate the preovulatory surge of GnRH through a robust di-synaptic pathway (Figure 12).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings, with reference to Figure 12.

claim: The differential release of amino acid and peptide neurotransmitters (segregated co-transmission) may occur at different release sites (ARH, median eminence, and AVPV/PeN) to coordinate reproductive function.
source: What is intriguing is the possibility that the differential release of amino acid and peptide neurotransmitters (segregated co-transmission) (Vaaga et al., 2014) occurs at these different release sites (ARH, median eminence, and AVPV/PeN) to coordinate reproductive function.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism, with a supporting citation.

claim: OVX animals exhibit increased GnRH and LH pulsatile secretion that coincide with increased expression of neuropeptides (including kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin) in ARH Kiss1 neurons.
source: It is well known that OVX animals exhibit increased GnRH and LH pulsatile secretion that coincide with increased expression of neuropeptides (including kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin) in ARH Kiss1 neurons (Caraty et al., 1989; Smith et al., 2005; Dellovade and Merchenthaler, 2004; Gottsch et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.
